case_identification.title: PortFlow Container Terminal: Yard and Gate Flow

case_inputs.brief: PortFlow is a Canadian container terminal linking shipping lines, trucking, rail and inland customers. Today the yard holds 21,120 TEU against 24,000 TEU effective capacity (88%), containers dwell 6 days, and trucks take 72 minutes per visit (40 queuing, 32 inside). Volume will grow 20% in five years. The terminal spends $6M a year on overtime and $8M on delay and service penalties. Release and schedule information is not shared consistently, planning runs across separate systems on fixed rules, and the yard system knows a container's stack but not its exact position. One 15-acre parcel (about 4,000 TEU) could be added, phased around live operations.
case_inputs.decision_question: Which package, within the $10M upfront budget, attacks PortFlow's core issue so that at +20% volume the yard runs at or below 85% utilization and trucks turn in under 45 minutes by year five?
case_inputs.objective: Year 5 at +20% volume: average yard utilization <= 85% and average truck turn time < 45 minutes, within $10M upfront.
case_inputs.baseline_metric: Year-5 yard utilization if nothing changes
constraints: Upfront investment at most $10M CAD; it does not need to be spent in full
Year-5 objectives: average yard utilization <= 85% and average truck turn time < 45 minutes
Vessel and truck operations cannot stop while changes are introduced
Customs holds and missing documentation cannot be overridden by PortFlow
Up to 8 content slides for a 10-minute presentation
case_inputs.suggested_analysis: Cause-versus-symptom tree, MIP block assignment, CRAFT layout improvement, demand forecasting

problem_diagnosis.core_bottleneck: The yard is static and blind. Today 21,120 of 24,000 TEU are in use (88%), containers stay 6 days and trucks take 72 minutes. With +20% volume the yard passes its capacity by year 5 unless containers are placed, moved and released faster; the 15-acre parcel alone would still leave about 90%.
problem_diagnosis.baseline_metric: Year-5 yard utilization if nothing changes
root_causes: Core issue (cause): the yard runs on fixed rules with incomplete data. Blocks are not zoned by demand, stacks ignore pickup order and exact position, the layout never adapts as demand shifts by season, and release status is not shared.
Wrong place: busy container groups sit far from the gate, rail and quay exits, so every move travels further (32 minutes inside).
Wrong order: stacks are built without knowing pickup time or exact slot, so cranes reshuffle boxes to dig out the one needed (rehandles and $6M overtime).
Wrong time: demand shifts (a product peaking in December but not in March) while the layout stays fixed, and customers learn late that boxes are released (6-day dwell, 40-minute queues).
Symptoms, not causes: yard crowding, $6M overtime, $8M penalties, customers unable to plan and staff anxiety.

red_team_defense.question: Why not just build on the 15-acre parcel?
red_team_defense.rebuttal: Space alone fails the objective: 25,344 / 28,000 TEU = 90.5% at year 5, for about $14.5M, over budget. Cutting dwell to 4.7 days reaches about 83% on today's footprint.

red_team_defense.question: Why only two AGVs?
red_team_defense.rebuttal: The evidence is mixed: successful automated terminals cut operating costs 25-55%, but some lose 7-15% productivity. Two units in a fenced lane prove uptime, cost per move and safety for $1.6M; the fleet grows only if the month-12 gate passes.

red_team_defense.question: How do the MIP and CRAFT work together?
red_team_defense.rebuttal: The MIP assigns container groups to blocks, minimising move frequency x distance to their exit within capacity and segregation rules. CRAFT then tries pairwise zone swaps and keeps any that lower total flow x distance, so the layout can be re-improved as demand shifts.

red_team_defense.question: What if the seasonal forecast is wrong?
red_team_defense.rebuttal: Slotting re-runs weekly on actual bookings, not only the forecast; planners approve every re-slot; zoning is reviewed monthly.

red_team_defense.question: How do you know where every container is?
red_team_defense.rebuttal: OCR cameras read container numbers at the gate and quay, crane position sensors record the exact slot of every pick and drop, and RFID tags identify each AGV and truck. Every move writes to one yard database that the slotting engine, the AGVs and the customer portal all read.

red_team_defense.question: Will automation cost jobs, and who maintains the AGVs?
red_team_defense.rebuttal: No layoffs from this program. Drivers can retrain as AGV supervisors and technicians. AGVs follow a preventive maintenance plan with a vendor SLA, and manual tractors stay as the fallback.

analysis_sections.title: Finance
points: Upfront $9.4M of the $10M budget, including $0.8M contingency; $0.6M left unspent.
Added annual costs $1.3M: software and database licences, sensors and AGV maintenance, model upkeep and refresher training.
AGV pricing: a US DOT-hosted study put one terminal AGV at about EUR 150,000 (2021, conservative). We budget $1.6M for 2 units including navigation, charging, fleet software and fencing.

Annual savings $6.4M with owners: overtime -40% ($2.4M, Operations Manager) from shorter travel, fewer rehandles and fewer re-plans; penalties -50% ($4.0M, Commercial Director) from reliable release information and faster truck service.
Five-year net impact = $9.4M + 5 x ($1.3M - $6.4M) = -$16.1M (net savings).
Uncertainty: the share of penalties caused by customs holds PortFlow cannot override. If penalties fall only 25%, the impact is still -$6.1M; break-even needs $3.2M a year.
deck_points: Savings owners: overtime -40% ($2.4M, Operations Manager); penalties -50% ($4.0M, Commercial Director)
AGVs are a $1.6M pilot; the fleet grows only if cost per move beats manual tractors

analysis_sections.title: Operations & Safety
points: Storage: shared release status and pickup windows cut dwell from 6.0 to 4.7 days, keeping year-5 utilization near 83% without new land.
Container movement: MIP/CRAFT zoning puts high-demand groups next to their exit; dynamic slotting stacks by pickup order, so cranes stop digging.
Truck service: queue 40 to about 15 min with pickup windows; time inside 32 to about 22 min with fast movers near the gate: about 37 minutes in total.
Safety: AGVs run only in a fenced lane; segregation rules for hazardous, reefer and weight are locked in the model; every go-live has a safety review.
Measures, reviewed weekly: utilization, dwell, rehandles per box, travel per move, queue and inside time, AGV uptime, incidents and near-misses.
deck_points: Zoning and slotting: fast movers near exits, stacks by pickup order
Trucks: queue 40 to ~15 min, inside 32 to ~22 min, about 37 min total
Safety: AGVs fenced; segregation rules locked; review at every go-live

analysis_sections.title: Supply Chain
points: Shipping lines: vessel ETA changes flow into the database and trigger re-slotting before the ship arrives.
Truckers: pickup windows only for released, ready containers, already staged near the gate.
Rail: rail-bound containers zoned next to the rail exit and staged by train departure.
Customers: release, hold and ETA alerts; seasonal demand signals (for example a December peak) feed the slotting forecast.
Customs holds stay outside PortFlow's control but are flagged early so no truck is booked against a held box.
deck_points: One database feeds lines, trucks, rail and customers
Customers' seasonal demand signals drive re-zoning ahead of peaks

analysis_sections.title: Organizational Change Management
points: Stakeholders: yard operators, tractor drivers, planners, maintenance, IT, truckers, rail, lines, customers and finance.
Involve staff before tools arrive: planners and operators co-design zones and slotting rules in phase 1.
Train in paid time: super-users per shift; tractor drivers can certify as AGV supervisors or technicians.
Clarify roles: no layoffs from this program; a RACI for every zone, model and AGV decision.
Keep operations running: one block re-zoned at a time, overnight moves, AGVs only in a fenced lane, rollback plan.
deck_points: Co-design before tools; paid training; drivers can become AGV supervisors
No layoffs; one block at a time; AGVs fenced

analysis_sections.title: AI & Automation
points: MIP: assigns container groups (customer, product, direction) to blocks to minimise move frequency x distance to their exit, within block capacity and segregation rules.
CRAFT: tests pairwise swaps of zones and keeps any swap that lowers total flow x distance, so the layout can be improved again as demand changes.
Dynamic slotting: a demand forecast (seasonal peaks) plus actual bookings re-slot containers weekly; planners approve each change.
AI AGVs: 2 battery units in a fenced quay-to-block lane, tracked by the yard database; overseen by the Engineering and Maintenance Manager with preventive maintenance.
Performance checks: 6 weeks of shadow mode for slotting; AGV uptime, cost per move and incidents weekly; scale the fleet only if the month-12 gate passes.
deck_points: MIP + CRAFT layout; weekly dynamic slotting; planners approve
2 AGVs piloted, maintained and measured before any scale-up

causes.law: What the case data shows: 21,120 of 24,000 TEU in use today (88%). Add 20% volume at today's 6-day stay and the yard needs about 25,300 TEU, more than it holds. Trucks take 72 minutes against a 45-minute objective, and overtime plus penalties cost $14M a year.

qa_bank.question: Why not Option A, the cheapest?
qa_bank.rebuttal: It costs CAD $1,600,000 but delivers 3.9% (misses the 19.5% target); it scores 5.22/10 vs 6.92/10 for Option B.

qa_bank.question: How confident are you in the option estimates?
qa_bank.rebuttal: Source: assumption: estimate (overtime -40%, penalties -50%; dwell 6.0 to 4.7 days). We treat them as hypotheses: the Horizon 1 pilot must reach 80% of the modelled gain before scale-up spend.

qa_bank.question: What does it cost to run every year?
qa_bank.rebuttal: O&M of CAD $1,300,000/yr is already netted out of the CAD $6,400,000/yr benefit.

qa_bank.question: What is the benefit-to-cost ratio?
qa_bank.rebuttal: 1.42 on a present-value basis at 9.5% WACC; levelized 134474.76 CAD per year per % point of improvement.

qa_bank.question: What if implementation takes 50% longer?
qa_bank.rebuttal: NPV falls to CAD $4,223,006; the H1 pilot and fixed-price packages protect the schedule.

qa_bank.question: How will you know it is working by day 30?
qa_bank.rebuttal: Pilot KPI: Move data cleaned; MIP/CRAFT layout validated in simulation; AGV vendor and safety case approved. Leading indicators: Constraint utilisation, OEE at the constraint.

qa_bank.question: What are the safety and regulatory implications?
qa_bank.rebuttal: Every change goes through management-of-change review and HAZOP before commissioning; designs are validated against local codes and vendor specifications, with licensed engineering review before deployment.

qa_bank.question: What would you do with 20% more budget?
qa_bank.rebuttal: Accelerate the rollout and add redundancy at the constraint.
